## What it is

Horizon is an unofficial, open-source reimplementation of Minecraft Java Edition written completely from scratch in Rust. Rather than wrapping or modifying the existing game binaries, it provides a native client and server stack designed to run vanilla saves, worlds, and resource packs without executing the Java Virtual Machine. It relies on a companion launcher to prepare necessary assets from an existing legitimate game installation.

## Why it matters

Traditional Java-based Minecraft instances demand heavy memory allocation and frequent garbage collection, limiting performance on lower-end hardware and complicating programmatic interaction. By shifting the engine to Rust, Horizon opens the door to high-performance rendering, lower memory overhead, and direct programmatic control for automation scripts and AI agents without relying on heavy third-party mod loaders.

## Key features

- Executes core game mechanics, world generation, and redstone natively in Rust.
- Ships with horizon-ctl and an MCP server interface for direct AI agent control.
- Supports distant terrain rendering up to 1024 chunks.
- Integrates with CurseForge and Modrinth data- and asset-based modpacks.
- Includes server management tools for local hosting or VPS deployments without Java.

## Quick start

To build and run the client from source after preparing your assets, use the following commands:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon.git
cd horizon
cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar
cargo run --release -p horizon-client
```

## Who should try it

Systems programmers, Rust enthusiasts, and advanced server administrators looking to experiment with low-level game engine architecture or build automated agents inside a sandbox environment will find plenty to explore here.

## Verdict

Horizon is an extraordinary technical achievement backed by rigorous differential testing. While it continues to close remaining parity gaps against vanilla releases, it serves as a compelling glimpse into what is possible when modern systems languages meet classic game design.

## What it is

Concat is a free, open-source video editor built in Rust as a local-first alternative to popular web-based and subscription tools. It provides multi-track editing, keyframes, auto-captions via Whisper, background removal, and a GPU-accelerated compositor that renders previews live. Rather than relying on cloud servers, the entire application runs locally on your desktop or mobile device, keeping your raw files entirely on disk.

## Why it matters

Most modern video editing tools force users into cloud uploads, opaque subscription tiers, or restrictive export limits. Concat removes these constraints by bringing the full editing pipeline into a self-hosted desktop environment. Furthermore, it bridges traditional video editing with modern developer tooling by exposing a JSON-RPC API and an MCP server, allowing scripts and AI assistants to programmatically manage timelines and cuts.

## Key features

- Run local Whisper auto-captions and voice cloning offline
- Composit GPU effects and transitions live in the preview
- Drive editing workflows via a built-in MCP server for AI agents
- Animate parameters with a built-in curve editor and keyframes
- Export to H.264, HEVC, and AV1 up to 4K 60fps in 10-bit color

## Quick start

To build and run Concat from source, ensure you have Rust 1.93+ and the FFmpeg development libraries installed, then run:

```sh
cd src
cargo run -p concat
```

## Who should try it

Developers, content creators, and automation engineers who want a capable video editor that runs entirely offline and can be scripted programmatically will find Concat worth evaluating.

## Verdict

Concat is a compelling option for anyone seeking an open-source, local-first video editor. While it remains in beta and has minor rough edges, its scriptability and lack of artificial paywalls make it a strong daily driver.

## Why it matters

When AI agents try to edit video using raw shell strings, they often guess codecs, assume frame rates, and fail silently. This project replaces guesswork with a structured workflow: probe the input file first, edit using typed arguments, and verify the output using local checks and visual contact sheets.

- Run 42 local video tools covering cuts, silence removal, captions, karaoke, and loudness normalisation
- Expose an MCP server with a machine-readable contract for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex
- Verify every execution automatically using built-in probing, checks, and visual contact sheets
- Operate fully offline without cloud dependencies, subscriptions, or external API keys
- Generate runtime input schemas directly from the CLI argparse definitions to prevent contract drift

```bash
npx ffmpeg-skill
```

## Who should try it

This tool fits developers building local media pipelines, automated video generation workflows, or leveraging AI coding assistants for local file manipulation.

## Verdict

An essential utility for anyone building local AI media workflows, provided you already have FFmpeg and Python installed.

## What it is

Filee is an open-source desktop file converter designed to handle 263 different formats entirely offline. Built using C# and Avalonia, it provides a unique interaction model: instead of opening a standalone application window, you hold a modifier key, drag your files, and drop them onto a format selection donut that appears right at your cursor. It operates locally, saving converted outputs directly next to the original files.

## Why it matters

For developers and power users, file conversion is often an annoying friction point. Existing solutions either require uploading sensitive files to random web services or spinning up bloated office suites. Filee removes this tradeoff by keeping everything on your local machine. It processes documents, images, archives, and media files without needing Microsoft Office, Hancom Office, or LibreOffice installed.

## Key features

- Trigger conversion menus by holding a modifier key and dropping files onto a cursor-anchored donut interface.
- Process over 260 formats locally without cloud uploads.
- Drag links or assets directly out of web browsers for instant conversion.
- Run parallel batch conversions with automatic routing for multi-step format transitions.
- Flip the format donut using the mouse wheel or Tab key to access alternative toolbars.
- Crop images, configure output quality, DPI, and watch folders for automated tasks.

## Quick start

To install Filee on Windows using WinGet, run:

```powershell
winget install KnifeLemon.Filee
```

## Who should try it

This tool is built for developers, designers, and system administrators who regularly juggle obscure file formats and want to keep their workflows entirely offline. Linux users should note that drag gestures currently require X11.

## Verdict

Filee is a polished, fast utility that eliminates the friction of file conversion. While certain platforms have minor limitations regarding drag gestures, its offline-first architecture makes it a great addition to any developer's local toolkit.

## What it is

Mika is an open-source on-device AI agent built for Android 11 and above. Written in Kotlin, it allows users to automate tasks across mobile applications and web pages by visually parsing UI elements rather than relying on app-specific APIs.

## How it works

The core architecture combines a background screen rendering engine with visual UI parsing and custom model integrations. Mika runs tasks on a hidden background screen, allowing users to continue interacting with their device normally while automation sequences execute. Additionally, it features an arm64 Linux sandbox to run Python, Node, and shell scripts per conversation.

## Key features

- Operates any Android app or website through visual screen parsing
- Runs tasks on a hidden background screen for uninterrupted phone usage
- Executes Python, Node, and shell scripts in a local sandbox
- Turns completed tasks into reusable skills with local memory
- Supports preset configurations or custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints

## Getting started

To run Mika, you will need an Android device running version 11 or higher, wireless debugging enabled, and your own model provider API keys or account login. Clone the repository from GitHub and follow the setup instructions to build and install the APK.

## When not to use it

Skip this tool if you prefer plug-and-play consumer apps that require zero configuration, or if you are not comfortable setting up wireless debugging and managing API keys.

Play your own Nintendo Switch games natively on iPhone and iPad. Bring your game (its NSP files) and your `prod.keys`; one script turns them into an IPA that you sideload.
